message.content:
The offset between Los Angeles (Pacific Time) and Berlin (Central European Time) normally stays constant at **9 hours** – Berlin is always ahead.  
However, because the two regions start and end daylight‑saving time on slightly different dates, there are short windows each year when the difference drops to **8 hours**:

| Period | Los Angeles | Berlin | Difference |
|--------|-------------|--------|------------|
| Standard time (winter) | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | +9 h |
| After LA enters DST but before Berlin does (late Mar) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| After Berlin exits DST but before LA does (late Oct) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| Daylight‑saving time (summer) | UTC‑7 | UTC+2 | +9 h |

So, for most of the year Berlin is 9 hours ahead of Los Angeles, but during the brief overlap periods around the DST transitions it’s 8 hours ahead.

During summer (DST): LA UTC-7, Berlin UTC+2 => difference 9 hours.

But there is a period when Berlin is on DST but LA hasn't started yet? Actually Berlin DST starts last Sunday in March; LA DST starts second Sunday in March. So Berlin DST starts after LA DST? So from March 12 to March 26, LA is on DST (UTC-7), Berlin is still on standard time (UTC+1). So difference then is 8 hours (Berlin ahead by 8 hours). Similarly, at end of DST: Berlin ends DST last Sunday in October; LA ends DST first Sunday in November. So from last Sunday in October to first Sunday in November, Berlin is on standard time (UTC+1), LA is still on DST (UTC-7). So difference again 8 hours. So difference varies between 8 and 9 hours depending on DST overlap.
